results.text:
Elasticsearch Metrics: 1,284 Commits, 17 Releases, and the Open-Core Tradeoff | ToolVitals

October 13, 2026 Databases by ToolVitals Research

# Elasticsearch Metrics: 1,284 Commits, 17 Releases, and the Open-Core Tradeoff

Elasticsearch is not showing a simple healthy-project story: ToolVitals records 1,284 GitHub commits in the last 30 days, 99 active contributors, a 98 health score, and a 98 shipping score. Yet the same payload reports 0 release events in 30 days, alongside 17 GitHub releases in 90 days. The gap is the real signal: development is busy, but the public release surface does not line up cleanly with that activity. Elasticsearch deserves evaluation as an active platform with a complicated delivery model, not as a star count with a database attached.

## Elasticsearch is broader than a search box

Elastic’s official Elasticsearch page positions the product as a distributed search, analytics, and AI platform. The page says Elasticsearch stores structured, unstructured, and vector data in real time, then supports full-text, hybrid, and vector search. It also presents observability and security analytics as central uses, not as unrelated add-ons.

The GitHub repository gives the same product a more engineering-focused description. It calls Elasticsearch a distributed search and analytics engine, a scalable data store, and a vector database optimized for speed and relevance on production-scale workloads. The repository also names retrieval-augmented generation and application performance monitoring as use cases.

That positioning changes the problem Elasticsearch is trying to solve. This is not only a document index for a search box. It is intended to keep multiple data types available for retrieval, analytics, monitoring, and AI-backed applications through a common system and API surface.

The benefit is architectural consolidation. A team can investigate one platform for text search, structured data, vectors, operational signals, and security data instead of assembling a separate product for each workload. The cost is evaluation complexity. A system that claims to serve several workload classes must be tested against each one, because a strong result in text search does not prove an equally strong result for vector retrieval, high-cardinality analytics, or operational monitoring.

## The metrics show activity, not a finished verdict

ToolVitals gives Elasticsearch a hot score of 216.7 and a ToolVitals score of 98. The repository has 78,227 GitHub stars, 1,284 commits in the 30-day window, 99 active contributors, and 17 GitHub releases in the 90-day window. Its health score is 98, its shipping score is 98, its 30-day release-event count is 0, and the payload assigns the data a confidence score of 90.

Those numbers support a clear claim about public project activity. Elasticsearch is not a dormant repository, and its development is spread across a large active contributor set. The high health and shipping scores also show that ToolVitals sees the project as well maintained and active according to its own measurements.

They do not support every conclusion a buyer might want. GitHub stars are accumulated attention, not a current usage count. A commit can represent a feature, a test, a refactor, documentation, a backport, or a merge. The active-contributor figure does not show how work is distributed across maintainers, vendors, or occasional contributors.

The release numbers need the same careful reading. ToolVitals reports 17 GitHub releases over 90 days but 0 release events over 30 days. The recent event data includes an Elasticsearch 9.5.2 GitHub release dated August 20, 2026, so the fields are clearly describing different windows or event definitions rather than one unified release counter. The safe interpretation is that Elasticsearch has substantial recent release history, while the current 30-day event metric does not show a release event.

作者：来自 Elastic Brian Bergholm

今天，我们很高兴地宣布 Elastic 8.14 正式发布。

## 什么是新的？

8.14 版本最重要的标题是 ES|QL 的正式发布(GA)，它是从头开始设计和专门构建的，可大大简化数据调查。在新的查询引擎的支持下，ES|QL 提供了具有并发处理的高级搜索功能，从而提高了速度和效率，而不受数据源和结构的影响。 8.14 版本的其他重要组成部分包括向量搜索改进的 GA 以及新的生成式 AI 攻击发现安全功能的技术预览。解决方案的其他亮点包括以下内容。

Elastic Search 帮助开发人员实现现代搜索和发现体验。

- 了解由于标量量化和向量优化超大规模硬件配置文件的正式发布带来的向量搜索显着的速度提升和成本节省、Elastic with OpenAI 和 Azure OpenAI 的综合检索增强生成 (RAG) 工具的技术预览、用于提取、转换数据并将数据加载到 Elastic 中的大量工具增强功能，以及 Elastic Search 亮点博客或 8.14 发行说明中的​​更多内容。

Elastic Observability 将指标、日志和跟踪转化为可操作的 IT 见解，以统一整个数字生态系统的可观察性。

- 请在 Elastic Observability 亮点博客或 8.14 发行说明中了解有关跨集群 SLO、增强型警报和合成的增强型 SLO 管理的 GA、增强型 AI 助手功能的 GA 等更多信息。

Elastic Security 统一了 SIEM、端点安全和云安全，以检测、调查和响应云规模的威胁。

- 了解新的生成式 AI 攻击发现的技术预览，以查明环境中最紧迫的威胁、对其他 LLM 和 AI 助手功能的支持的 GA 以及 Elastic Security 亮点博客中的更多信息或 8.14 发行说明中的​​详细信息。

Elastic 的所有开箱即用解决方案均构建在 Elasticsearch 平台上。所有用户，无论使用情况如何，都可以从核心增强功能中受益。

- 了解 CCS/CCR 基于 API 密钥的安全模型的正式发布、对选定 MaxMind 地理定位数据库的额外支持以及数据流生命周期功能的正式发布。
- 另外值得注意的是，请阅读 ECK 上 Logstash 的 GA、AWS 中使用客户管理密钥进行静态加密的 GA，以及 Elasticsearch 平台亮点博客或 8.14 发行说明中的​​更多信息。

## 从今天开始

准备好开始了吗？ Elastic 8.14 现已在 Elastic Cloud 上推出，Elastic Cloud 是托管的 Elasticsearch 服务，包含此最新版本中的所有新功能。

> 本文中描述的任何特性或功能的发布和时间安排均由 Elastic 自行决定。当前不可用的任何特性或功能可能无法按时交付或根本无法交付。

原文：Elastic 8.14: Announcing the GA of Elasticsearch Query Language (ES|QL) | Elastic Blog

Loki vs. Elasticsearch in 2026: Object-Store Log Economics Measured on Real Disk — Platform Monkey

# Loki vs. Elasticsearch in 2026: Object-Store Log Economics Measured on Real Disk

 September 19, 2026 · By Yuval Glasman 

Sources

- Loki v3.7.8 release (Sep 17, 2026) — security fixes to grpc, containerd, x/net, x/crypto
- Loki v3.7.0 release — new query engine scheduler capacity changes, dataobj partitions
- Elasticsearch 9.5.4 release (Sep 15, 2026) — current stable
- Elasticsearch 9.5.0 release notes — columnar and logsdb_columnar index modes (Tech Preview)
- Elastic docs — Logs data streams: logsdb enabled by default in Elastic Stack 9.0+, up to 60% storage reduction, 10-20% indexing impact
- Elastic logsdb GA announcement — Dec 2024, up to 65% storage reduction vs non-logsdb
- Loki 3.7 upgrade notes — BREAKING CHANGES: scheduler compute capacity, shared worker threads, parsed labels vs structured metadata
- Grafana Loki Helm chart index — chart 7.x series, appVersion 3.6.x (Sep 2026)

September 19, 2026. Loki 3.7.8 landed on September 17 — a security-patch release (gRPC, containerd, x/crypto CVE bumps, no fanfare). Elasticsearch 9.5.4 shipped two days earlier on September 15. Neither event made headlines, which is exactly why this comparison needed redoing: the last time most teams seriously evaluated Loki against Elasticsearch, Elastic had nothing like Loki’s object-store economics, and Loki had nothing like Elasticsearch’s query engine. In 2026 both halves of that sentence are wrong, and almost nobody has re-run the numbers.

So we did. We generated a realistic 300,000-line Kubernetes-style log corpus (40.9 MB of raw log-line payload: API access logs across 4 namespaces, 9 pods, INFO/WARN/ERROR levels, HTTP routes, status codes, latencies, plus the kind of operational chatter real pods emit), pushed the identical corpus into a single-binary Loki 3.7.8 (TSDB schema, filesystem object store) and a single-node Elasticsearch 9.5.4, and measured what actually hit disk. Then we repeated the Elasticsearch run in its brand-new `logsdb_columnar` index mode — the Tech Preview Elastic shipped in 9.5.0 that turns the “Loki is cheaper” argument into a live engineering question.

The headline: on identical data, Loki stored the corpus in 10.1 MB (4.1× compression), standard logsdb Elasticsearch took 52.6 MB (129% of raw), and logsdb_columnar took 7.9 MB with keyword-mapped message fields — but only 32.4 MB (79% of raw) once we mapped the message field as `text` so phrase search actually works. Every number in this guide comes from the bench we ran; the exact methodology is below so you can reproduce it.

## TL;DR — The Verdict First

- Log volume is your primary cost, and the storage profiles have converged — but not the query engines. Loki’s TSDB+chunk pipeline compressed our corpus 4.1×. Elasticsearch’s default logsdb mode stored 129% of raw bytes. logsdb_columnar with an all-keyword schema got to 5.2× — nominally smaller than Loki — but the moment you give the message field an inverted index (so full-text search works), it lands at 79% of raw: still 3.2× bigger than Loki.
- Query latency is the mirror image. On a needle-in-haystack phrase search across 300k lines, Elasticsearch answered in 35 ms where Loki took 280 ms — 8× faster on a single-node toy. That gap is structural: Elasticsearch reads an inverted index, Loki greps compressed chunk data. At petabyte scale Loki’s parallelism closes some of the distance, but you should never adopt Loki expecting Elasticsearch-class ad-hoc search latency.
- Memory is the hidden Elasticsearch line item. Our single-node bench Elasticsearch settled at 2.0 GB RSS with a 2 GB heap. Loki settled at 0.12 GB RSS doing the same ingestion work. That 16× ratio is why “just use Elasticsearch for logs” fleets keep growing JVM heaps faster than their log volume grows.
